title: John Prepares the Way, and the Son Is Named
summary: In a year carefully dated by the rulers of the day, the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. He calls Israel to a baptism of repentance, tells ordinary people what fruit that repentance should bear, and points to a coming one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire, before Herod silences him in prison. Jesus is baptized, the Spirit descends, the Father's voice names him beloved Son, and Luke traces his line all the way back to Adam and to God.
story:
Luke's first two chapters told of two births, John's and Jesus', and ended with the boy Jesus in the temple. Now roughly eighteen years pass in silence and both sons are grown. The prophetic voice that fell quiet in Israel returns with John, introduced in the words used for Jeremiah and Hosea, and his work is to get a people ready. Then the story turns to Jesus. At his baptism heaven itself declares who he is, and the genealogy that follows sets that declaration inside the whole human story, from Joseph back through David and Abraham to Adam, son of God.

The chapter is a hinge. It closes the story of John, whom Luke removes to prison before he narrates Jesus' baptism, and it opens the public ministry of Jesus, which begins in chapter 4 with the temptation in the wilderness and the sermon at Nazareth. The title the Father speaks at the Jordan, beloved Son, is the title the devil will test (If You are the Son of God, 4:3 and 4:9), and the Spirit who descends on Jesus here is the Spirit he announces at Nazareth (4:18). John's promise that the coming one will baptize with the Holy Spirit is fulfilled only at the end of Luke's story, at Pentecost (Acts 1:5, 2:33).
historical:
Luke dates John's call the way ancient historians dated events, by the officeholders of the year, and he does it more elaborately than any other New Testament writer. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in August AD 14, so his fifteenth year falls in late AD 28 or 29, depending on whether Luke counted by the Roman calendar or a Syrian one. Some count instead from AD 12, when Tiberius began sharing provincial authority with Augustus (Velleius Paterculus 2.121), arriving at about AD 26 or 27, which fits better with a crucifixion in AD 30. Pontius Pilate governed Judea from about AD 26 to 36; a limestone block found in the theater at Caesarea in 1961 bears his name and gives his title as praefectus, prefect.

After Herod the Great died, about 4 BC, Augustus divided his kingdom among three sons. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea as tetrarch (a ruler of part of a divided territory, below a king) from 4 BC until Caligula exiled him in AD 39 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.252). Philip ruled the lands northeast of the Sea of Galilee, Ituraea and Trachonitis, until his death in the twentieth year of Tiberius, AD 33 or 34 (Antiquities 18.106). Archelaus, the third son, ruled Judea until AD 6, when Rome deposed him and sent a prefect. Lysanias of Abilene, north of Damascus, was once thought to be Luke's error, since the best-known Lysanias was executed at Mark Antony's order in the 30s BC; but Josephus speaks of Abila of Lysanias (Antiquities 19.275), and an inscription from Abila, set up between AD 14 and 29 for the safety of the lords Augusti (Tiberius and his mother Livia), names a freedman of Lysanias the tetrarch, pointing to a later ruler of that name in Luke's period.

Annas had been appointed high priest by Quirinius in AD 6 and removed by the prefect Valerius Gratus about AD 15 (Antiquities 18.26, 18.34), but five of his sons later held the office (Antiquities 20.198) and his son-in-law Joseph Caiaphas served from about AD 18 to 36. Luke names both, with a singular high priesthood, because Annas remained the power behind the office, as John 18:13 and Acts 4:6 also show. In 1990 a family tomb south of the Old City yielded an ornate ossuary (bone box) inscribed Yehosef bar Qayafa, which many scholars take to belong to Caiaphas's family.

Josephus tells of John the Baptist independently (Antiquities 18.116-119). He calls John a good man who urged Jews to practice virtue, justice toward one another, and piety toward God, and to come to baptism, and he says Antipas, fearing that John's influence over the crowds might lead to revolt, sent him in chains to the fortress of Machaerus, east of the Dead Sea, and put him to death. Josephus mentions the story because many Jews saw Antipas's defeat by the Nabatean king Aretas IV in AD 36 as God's punishment for killing John. Aretas's quarrel began when Antipas divorced Aretas's daughter to marry Herodias, the wife of his half-brother (Antiquities 18.109-110), the marriage Luke says John rebuked, since the Law forbade marrying a brother's wife while he lived (Leviticus 18:16, 20:21).
cultural:
Ritual washing was common in Judaism of the Second Temple period, the era from the rebuilding of the temple in the late sixth century BC to its destruction in AD 70. Stepped immersion pools (miqva'ot) have been found near the Temple Mount, in the mansions of Jerusalem's priestly quarter, and at Qumran, whose community practiced repeated purifications and insisted that washing had no effect without a turning from sin (1QS 3:4-9, 5:13-14). John's baptism was different in three ways: it was a single act rather than a repeated one, it was administered by John rather than self-immersion, and it was tied to repentance and forgiveness for Israelites, who did not usually think they needed the kind of rite later given to Gentile converts. The Mishnah records a debate between the schools of Hillel and Shammai about a proselyte's immersion (m. Pesahim 8:8), though how early proselyte baptism began is disputed. Joan Taylor (The Immerser, 1997) places John firmly within this world of Jewish purification.

John's warning, “We have Abraham as our father”, strikes at a real conviction. Descent from Abraham was Israel's glory (Isaiah 51:1-2), and the Mishnah later states that all Israel has a share in the world to come (m. Sanhedrin 10:1). John, like the prophets before him, insists that belonging must be shown in fruit, and he plays on words: in Hebrew and Aramaic, stones (avanim) and children (banim) sound alike.

The people who ask what to do are concrete figures. Tax collectors (telōnai) in Galilee and Judea mostly collected tolls and customs on goods, working for contractors who bid for the right to collect in a district and profited from whatever they collected above the fixed amount. The system invited overcharging, and Jewish collectors were despised as extortioners and collaborators; the Mishnah even permits a man to make a false vow to escape a tax collector (m. Nedarim 3:4). The soldiers were probably not Roman legionaries, since no legion was stationed in Judea or Galilee before AD 66, but troops of Antipas or auxiliaries recruited locally to support the authorities and the tax system, often ill-paid and tempted to live off the population. Carrying or untying a master's sandals was a slave's task; a later saying attributed to Rabbi Joshua ben Levi holds that a disciple should do for his teacher everything a slave does except untying his sandal (b. Ketubot 96a), so John places himself below a slave before the coming one. A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind so the heavy wheat fell to the threshing floor and the chaff blew aside to be gathered and burned.

Genealogies mattered in this world. Priests had to prove their descent, and Josephus opens his autobiography with his own priestly and royal lineage, as he found it in the public records (Life 1-6); he says priestly families kept their genealogies in archives (Against Apion 1.31-36). Julius Africanus later reported that Herod burned the genealogical records of Jewish families, but that some families, including the relatives of Jesus, kept private records (Eusebius, Church History 1.7). About thirty was a recognized age for taking up public work: Joseph entered Pharaoh's service at thirty (Genesis 41:46), David began to reign at thirty (2 Samuel 5:4), and Levites served from thirty (Numbers 4:3).
literary:
The chapter opens like a prophetic book: “the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness” echoes the openings of Jeremiah (1:1-3) and Hosea (1:1), which date the prophet's call by the kings of the day. Luke quotes Isaiah 40:3-5 at greater length than Matthew 3 or Mark 1, carrying it through the leveling of valleys and hills to “And all humanity will see God’s salvation,” because that universal note runs through his whole work, from Simeon's song (2:30-32) to Paul's last words in Rome (Acts 28:28).

John's preaching comes in three parts: warning to the crowds (verses 7 to 9), practical instruction found only in Luke (verses 10 to 14), and messianic promise (verses 15 to 17). The middle section is built on a threefold question, What then should we do?, asked by the crowds, the tax collectors, and the soldiers, and each receives an answer fitted to its own life. Luke then summarizes all this as good news (verse 18), and reports John's imprisonment (verses 19 and 20) before the baptism of Jesus, clearing the stage even though the arrest happened later, as Mark 6:17-18 shows. Hans Conzelmann (1954) read this rearrangement as a sign that Luke placed John in the old epoch of Israel, before the middle of time that begins with Jesus (compare 16:16); others think Luke simply finishes one character's story before starting another's, as he does in 1:56.

The baptism itself is told in a subordinate clause: all the people had been baptized, Jesus had been baptized, and while he was praying heaven opened. The weight falls on what follows, the Spirit's descent in bodily form and the Father's voice, and on the note, found only in Luke, that Jesus was praying. The genealogy then runs backward, son of, son of, name after name, a different design from Matthew's forward list in three groups of fourteen. It ends with “the son of Adam, the son of God,” echoing the voice at the baptism and leading straight into the temptation, where the new Son of God resists the tempter as Adam did not.

outline.t: The word of God comes to John in the wilderness
Warning to the crowds: bear fruit
What repentance looks like for crowds, tax collectors, and soldiers
The one more powerful who is coming
The genealogy of Jesus from Joseph to Adam

doctrines.note: Repentance in this chapter is a turning that shows up in behavior: sharing clothing and food, honest collection, no extortion or false accusation, contentment with wages. John joins it to baptism and to the forgiveness of sins (verse 3), and he refuses to let ancestry or religious identity replace it (verse 8). Luke even calls the call to repent good news (verse 18), because it comes before the judgment, not after.

At the baptism the Son prays, the Spirit descends in bodily form, and the Father speaks from heaven (verses 21-22). The church fathers cited this scene constantly as a revelation of the three persons of the one God acting together and distinctly, and the Eastern churches call the feast of the baptism the Theophany, the appearing of God.

John speaks of coming wrath, an axe already at the root, and chaff burned in unquenchable fire. The coming one both baptizes with the Spirit and sorts the harvest. Judgment here is near and falls on fruitlessness, and the warning is meant to produce the fruit that escapes it.

The voice from heaven joins the royal Son of Psalm 2:7 with the servant of Isaiah 42:1, on whom God puts his Spirit. Jesus is anointed with the Spirit for his work (4:18, Acts 10:38), king and servant in one person, and the genealogy confirms that he is David's descendant, as the promise required (2 Samuel 7:12).

Luke traces Jesus past Abraham to Adam, whom he calls “the son of God” (verse 38). Adam is God's son because he was made in God's image and likeness (Genesis 5:1-3). The genealogy places the true Son of God at the end of a line that began with the first, and prepares for the New Testament's teaching that Jesus is the last Adam and the true image of God (1 Corinthians 15:45, Colossians 1:15).

words.note: Rhēma, word, saying, and sometimes the thing spoken of. It occurs about sixty-eight times in the New Testament, nearly half of them in Luke and Acts. In verse 2 the word of God comes to John, the phrase of the Septuagint's Jeremiah 1:1, where Luke could have used logos. Like Hebrew davar, rhēma can mean both a message and an event (2:15), and here it marks John's ministry as God's own initiative, not a movement John began.

Metanoia, repentance. It occurs twenty-two times in the New Testament, half of them in Luke and Acts. The word suggests a change of mind, but in the Greek Bible and in John's preaching it carries the Hebrew idea of turning back to God (shuv). BDAG describes it as a change of mind and heart that includes remorse and a new direction. Luke insists it has fruit, visible changes in how people handle money, power, and possessions (verses 8 and 10-14), and the risen Jesus sends his disciples to preach it to all nations (24:47).

Aphesis, release, forgiveness. It occurs seventeen times in the New Testament, ten of them in Luke and Acts. In the Septuagint it names the release of the Jubilee year (Leviticus 25:10) and the release of debts, and Luke uses it twice in Jesus' reading of Isaiah at Nazareth for freedom for the captives (4:18). John's baptism is for the aphesis of sins (verse 3), so forgiveness is pictured as a release, the cancellation of a debt, which Luke joins with repentance in the church's preaching (24:47, Acts 2:38).

Karpos, fruit. It occurs about sixty-six times in the New Testament, often as a picture of the life that shows what a person is (6:43-44, Galatians 5:22). John demands fruit in keeping with repentance (verse 8) and warns that every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down (verse 9). The image comes from the prophets' vineyard and orchard (Isaiah 5:1-7) and returns in Jesus' parable of the fig tree given one more year (13:6-9).

Baptizō, to dip, immerse, wash. It occurs about seventy-seven times in the New Testament and could describe washing as well as plunging; Luke uses it of Jewish ritual hand-washing in 11:38. John uses the same verb for his own water baptism and for the coming one's baptism with the Holy Spirit and fire, which Luke shows poured out at Pentecost in Acts 2. The mode and meaning of Christian baptism are debated among the churches; this chapter describes John's baptism, a sign of repentance, and points beyond it to the Spirit.

Pur, fire. It occurs about seventy-one times in the New Testament and three times in this chapter (verses 9, 16, 17). Fire can purify (Malachi 3:2-3) or destroy (Isaiah 66:24), and John uses both senses: unfruitful trees are thrown into the fire, the chaff burns with unquenchable fire, and the coming one baptizes with the Holy Spirit and fire. Interpreters differ on whether the last means one purifying and judging baptism, as James Dunn argued (1970), the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3), or judgment for the unrepentant alongside the Spirit for the repentant.

Agapētos, beloved. It occurs about sixty times in the New Testament, often of believers, but in the Gospels mainly in the Father's words at the baptism and transfiguration and in the parable of the vineyard owner's beloved son (20:13). In the Septuagint it often means an only or uniquely cherished child: Isaac is Abraham's beloved son in Genesis 22:2. The Father's words echo Psalm 2:7, where God addresses his anointed king as son, and Isaiah 42:1, where God delights in his chosen servant.

Nomizō, to think, suppose, or regard, and in some contexts to hold by custom or law. It occurs fifteen times in the New Testament, nine of them in Luke and Acts (2:44 of Jesus' parents assuming he was in their company). In verse 23 Jesus was regarded, or supposed, to be the son of Joseph. The word acknowledges both that Joseph was Jesus' legal father and heir-giver and that, as Luke 1 has told, he was not conceived by Joseph.

christ:
The chapter shows who Jesus is through two witnesses. John, whom Jesus will call greater than any born of women (7:28), says he is not worthy to untie the straps of this man's sandals, and that the coming one will do what no prophet could: baptize with God's own Spirit and carry out God's own judgment. The one who comes after John is the Lord for whom Isaiah's voice prepares the way (verse 4). Luke quotes Isaiah 40:3 but changes ‘the paths of our God’ to ‘His paths’, so that the Lord whose way is prepared can be Jesus; the verse that promised God's own return to Zion now introduces Jesus.

Then heaven speaks: “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.” The sentence gathers three strands of Old Testament hope. Psalm 2:7 is a coronation oracle for David's heir; beloved recalls Isaac, the only son of Genesis 22:2; and ‘well pleased’ echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God's chosen servant, on whom he puts his Spirit, will bring justice to the nations. Jesus is king, beloved son, and Spirit-anointed servant in one person. Luke notes that he was praying when heaven opened, the first of many moments where he shows Jesus at prayer (5:16, 6:12, 9:18, 9:28-29, 22:41-44, 23:46).

By joining the crowds in a baptism of repentance, the sinless Son stands with sinners from the first day of his ministry, the solidarity that will lead him to be counted among the lawless (22:37) and to die between two criminals. The genealogy extends that solidarity to everyone. Matthew traces Jesus to Abraham, the father of Israel; Luke traces him to Adam, so that he belongs to the whole human family, and to God, so that he is the Son who will succeed where Adam failed. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.22.3) saw in this the recapitulation of humanity: Christ sums up in himself all the nations descended from Adam, and undoes Adam's disobedience by his obedience. Paul makes the same contrast between Adam and Christ in Romans 5:12-21 and 1 Corinthians 15:45.
interpretation:
The baptism of Jesus was among the most discussed scenes of the early church. Some early groups read it as the moment Jesus became God's Son. The Gospel of the Ebionites, as quoted by Epiphanius (Panarion 30.13), had the voice say ‘today I have begotten you’, as Codex Bezae does in Luke 3:22, and Theodotus the Cobbler, excommunicated in Rome around 190, taught that the Spirit came on a mere man at the Jordan (Eusebius, Church History 5.28). The church answered that the Son is eternal and that the baptism revealed rather than created his sonship. The Gospel of the Nazarenes, quoted by Jerome (Against Pelagius 3.2), has Jesus ask what sin he had committed that he should be baptized, showing that the question of verse 21 was felt early. Gregory of Nazianzus's Oration 39, On the Holy Lights (381), taught that Christ was baptized not to be cleansed but to cleanse the waters, and Ambrose and Augustine taught the same in the West. The Eastern churches keep 6 January as the Theophany with the Great Blessing of the Waters, and the Western churches keep the Baptism of the Lord in the Epiphany season.

The genealogy drew its own tradition. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.22.3) counted seventy-two generations and read them as Christ gathering up all the nations and languages descended from Adam. Julius Africanus's letter to Aristides, preserved by Eusebius (Church History 1.7), explained the difference from Matthew by levirate marriage. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.1-4) first explained it by adoption and later accepted Africanus's account. Around 1490 Annius of Viterbo proposed that Luke gives Mary's line, a view that spread in the sixteenth century and is still widely held among evangelicals.

Jewish tradition preserves John in Josephus's account, which gives a different emphasis from the Gospels: John's baptism purified the body for those whose souls were already cleansed by righteousness. The rabbis never mention him. The Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran, a small baptizing religion whose sacred books were written down centuries later, venerate John as a prophet. Modern Jewish and Christian historians, Joan Taylor (The Immerser, 1997) among them, place John within the purity practices of Second Temple Judaism, and John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, volume 2, 1994) counts Jesus' baptism by John among the most certain facts about him, since the early church found it embarrassing.

John's answer to the soldiers in verse 14 became a text in the church's long argument about war: Tertullian (On Idolatry 19) doubted that a Christian could serve as a soldier at all, while Augustine (Letter 189, to Boniface) cited the verse to argue that military service is not in itself forbidden. The Reformers saw in John the pattern of the preacher of repentance who points away from himself. Luther's baptismal hymn Christ unser Herr zum Jordan kam (1541) became the basis of Bach's cantata for the feast of John the Baptist in 1724 (BWV 7). In art the scene was painted by Piero della Francesca (The Baptism of Christ, about 1450s, National Gallery, London) and by Andrea del Verrocchio with the young Leonardo (about 1472 to 1475, Uffizi). Hans Conzelmann's reading of verses 19 and 20 (1954) made the chapter central to the modern study of Luke's theology of history. In the Revised Common Lectionary, Year C reads verses 1 to 6 on the second Sunday of Advent, verses 7 to 18 on the third, and verses 15 to 17 and 21 to 22 on the Baptism of the Lord.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from the manuscripts. In verse 22 Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts read Psalm 2:7 in full: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’, a wording Justin Martyr knew (Dialogue with Trypho 88, 103). Bart Ehrman (The Orthodox Corruption of Scripture, 1993) argued this is original and was changed because it could sound as if Jesus became God's Son at his baptism; most editors keep the reading of the great majority of manuscripts, which agrees with Mark 1:11. Codex Bezae also replaces Luke's names from Joseph to David (verses 23 to 31) with Matthew's list, reversed to fit Luke's order, one of the longest variants in the Gospels.

In verse 2 the Byzantine manuscripts read ‘the high priests’ (so the King James Version), smoothing the singular with two names. In verse 19 they add ‘Philip’ (‘Herodias his brother Philip's wife’), probably from Mark 6:17; the earliest manuscripts read simply ‘his brother's wife’. In verse 32 the earliest manuscripts read Sala where others read Salmon, the form in Ruth 4:20-21 and Matthew 1:4-5. Verse 33 survives in many variant forms: the critical editions print ‘Amminadab, Admin, Arni’, following early witnesses, while the Byzantine text reads ‘Aminadab, Aram’ to match Ram in Ruth 4:19 and Matthew 1:3-4. The second Cainan in verse 36 is absent from the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12-13 but present in the Septuagint and in Jubilees 8:1, so Luke followed his Greek Bible. In verses 4 to 6 Luke's quotation follows the Septuagint of Isaiah 40, which attaches ‘in the wilderness’ to the voice rather than to the road and ends with all flesh seeing the salvation of God.

teach.big: God's word breaks into history to prepare a people through a repentance that changes how they live, and then God himself names Jesus as his beloved Son, anointed by the Spirit, who stands with sinners and belongs to the whole human race.

outline.t: God's word comes to a real prophet at a real date, and his message is that God is coming and every obstacle must be cleared so that all people may see his salvation.
Religious heritage cannot replace repentance, and judgment is near for any life that bears no fruit.
Repentance is concrete and fitted to each life: generosity for the comfortable, honesty for the one who handles money, restraint for the one who holds power.
The greatest prophet points away from himself to one stronger, who gives the Spirit and carries out God's judgment, and even the warning is good news.
Faithful witness can cost everything, and John's imprisonment shows the price of calling the powerful to account.
Jesus stands with sinners in their baptism, prays, and receives the Spirit and the Father's word: he is the beloved Son, king and servant.
Jesus belongs to David's house, to Abraham's family, and to the whole human race descended from Adam, and he is the true Son of God who will succeed where Adam failed.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first treats John's instructions as a complete ethic or a means of earning God's favor. They are the fruit of repentance, not its substitute, and they are addressed to specific people in specific jobs; the point is that repentance reaches into daily work, not that sharing a tunic saves. The second turns John into a merely harsh preacher and misses that Luke calls his message good news. The third uses the baptism to argue for one mode or age of Christian baptism; the chapter describes John's baptism of repentance, and the churches' debates about baptism need to be argued from the whole New Testament, not settled here.

With the baptism of Jesus, avoid suggesting that Jesus needed forgiveness or that he became God's Son at that moment; Luke has already said he is the Son from his conception (1:35). With the genealogy, avoid skipping it as dull and avoid forcing a single harmonization with Matthew as if it were the only faithful view. The list has a clear purpose: to show that Jesus belongs to Israel and to all humanity, and to lead the reader from Adam, son of God, to the temptation.
teach.pastoral: John's words to tax collectors and soldiers press on people whose work tempts them to cheat, exploit, or abuse power, and some will feel exposed. Teach it as an invitation to change within their callings, not as a sentence of condemnation. The genealogy may press on those who do not know their family history, were adopted, or grew up without a father: Jesus himself was regarded as the son of Joseph, and his line runs finally to God, which can speak to anyone whose earthly family is broken or unknown. And those who fear they have fallen too far should hear that Jesus began his ministry by standing in line with sinners at the river.

hard.q: Why do Luke's and Matthew's genealogies of Jesus disagree?
hard.a:
The objection is plain. The two lists run closely together from Abraham to David (the main difference is that Luke's text, following the best manuscripts, has Admin and Arni in verse 33 where Matthew has Ram) but then divide. Matthew traces the line through Solomon and the kings of Judah and names Jacob as Joseph's father; Luke traces it through another son of David, Nathan, and names Heli. The two lists meet at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel and part again, and even there Luke makes Shealtiel the son of Neri while Matthew and 1 Chronicles 3:17 make him the son of Jeconiah. Luke also counts many more generations between David and Jesus than Matthew does. David Friedrich Strauss (1835) took the conflict as proof that neither list is historical, and critical scholars such as Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) and Joseph Fitzmyer (1981) conclude that the evangelists drew on different traditions and shaped them for theological ends: Matthew's royal line in three groups of fourteen, Luke's universal line reaching to Adam in seventy-seven generations. On this view they cannot be fully harmonized.

Three main harmonizing explanations have been offered. The oldest, from Julius Africanus in the early third century (Eusebius, Church History 1.7), holds that both lists are Joseph's: Jacob and Heli were half-brothers with the same mother, Heli died childless, and Jacob married his widow and raised up Joseph in Heli's name, so that Joseph was Jacob's son by nature and Heli's by law. Africanus said the account came from Jesus' relatives, and Augustine came to accept it. A second, proposed by Annius of Viterbo around 1490 and defended by many later commentators, holds that Luke gives Mary's line: Heli was Mary's father, and Joseph is called his son as a son-in-law; Frédéric Godet argued that the missing article before Joseph's name in the Greek supports this, and defenders add that it lets Luke's line avoid Jeconiah, whose descendants Jeremiah 22:30 excludes from David's throne. A third, argued by J. Gresham Machen (The Virgin Birth of Christ, 1930), holds that Matthew gives the legal line of succession to David's throne and Luke the actual descent of Joseph. Richard Bauckham (Jude and the Relatives of Jesus in the Early Church, 1990) has argued that Luke's list, with its pattern of seventy-seven generations, reflects traditions preserved among Jesus' own relatives. Each view has defenders who take Scripture seriously, and none is required by the church's confession. What both genealogies plainly affirm is that Jesus comes from David's house and from Abraham's family, and Luke adds that he belongs to all humanity.

hard.q: If Jesus was sinless, why was he baptized with a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins?
hard.a:
The objection has been felt from the beginning. John's baptism is described as ‘a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins’ (verse 3), and to submit to it seems to admit sin and to place Jesus beneath John. The Gospel of the Nazarenes, as quoted by Jerome (Against Pelagius 3.2), already has Jesus ask what sin he had committed that he should go and be baptized. Modern historians, John P. Meier among them (A Marginal Jew, volume 2, 1994), use the baptism as a prime example of the criterion of embarrassment: the early church would not have invented a story that made Jesus look like John's penitent disciple, so it almost certainly happened. Some go further and argue that the historical Jesus began as a follower of John who shared his call to repentance, and that the Gospels progressively softened the story: Mark tells it plainly, Matthew adds John's protest (Matthew 3:14-15), Luke mentions it in a subordinate clause after removing John from the scene, and John's Gospel does not narrate the baptism at all.

Christian interpreters answer in several ways. Matthew's account gives Jesus' own reason, to fulfill all righteousness (Matthew 3:15), which many read as his identification with the people of God in their obedience to God's call. The fathers, from Ignatius (To the Ephesians 18) to Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 39), taught that he was baptized not to be cleansed but to sanctify the waters for the church's baptism. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae III, question 39) gave a series of reasons, among them that Christ was baptized to show his humility and to consecrate baptism, and Calvin read the event as the solidarity of the one who came to bear the sins of others. Many modern scholars see the baptism as the first act of the servant who is counted among transgressors (Isaiah 53:12, quoted in Luke 22:37). Luke's own telling shifts the emphasis from the rite to what follows it: the prayer, the Spirit, and the voice. On the historical question, critics and believers agree that Jesus was baptized by John; they differ over how he understood it, and the Gospels invite the reader to see it through the Father's verdict: “in You I am well pleased.”

observe: List the rulers and priests Luke names in verses 1-2. Why might he date John's call so carefully?
What three groups ask John “What then should we do?” and what does he tell each of them?
What three things happen after Jesus is baptized while he is praying (verses 21-22), and how does the genealogy end (verse 38)?
interpret: Why does John refuse to let the crowds rely on having Abraham as their father? What does he mean by fruit in keeping with repentance?
What do the Father's words at the baptism draw from Psalm 2 and Isaiah 42, and what do they reveal about the kind of Messiah Jesus will be?
Why might Luke trace Jesus' ancestry back to Adam rather than stopping at Abraham, and why place the genealogy between the baptism and the temptation?
apply: John's answers to the crowds, the tax collectors, and the soldiers are specific to their situations. What would his answer be to someone in your work or position?
What kinds of inherited identity (family, church, nation) do people rely on today the way John's hearers relied on having Abraham as their father?
Jesus begins his ministry by standing in line with sinners at the river. What does that tell you about how he approaches you and the people you find hardest to love?
